'''''Lilium lancifolium''''' (syn. ''L. tigrinum'') is an Asian species of [[Lilium|lily]], native to [[China]], [[Japan]], [[Korea]], and the [[Russian Far East]].<ref name=POWO_537628-1/> It is widely planted as an ornamental because of its showy orange-and-black flowers, and sporadically occurs as a [[garden escapee]] in North America, particularly the eastern United States including New England,<ref name=flora-of-northamerica-online/> and has made incursions into some southern states such as Georgia.<ref>[https://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Lilium%20lancifolium.png Biota of North America Program 2014 county distribution map]</ref>

It has the English name '''tiger lily''', but that name has been applied to other species as well. 
[[File:Lilium tigrinum 005.jpg|thumb|right|''Lilium lancifolium'', [[Batiscan, Quebec#Photos - Batiscan|Batiscan]], [[Quebec]], [[Canada]]]]

== Description ==
[[File:Lilium lancifolium bulbils2.jpg|thumb|Leaf axil bulbils with developing roots in late summer]]
Like other true lilies, the [[flower]]s are borne on upright stems that are {{convert|80|-|200|cm|abbr=off}} tall and bear lanceolate [[leaves]] {{convert|6|-|10|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} long and {{convert|1|-|2|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}} broad. ''L. lancifolium'' produces aerial [[bulb]]lets, known as [[bulb]]ils, in the [[leaf axils]].<ref name="ohwi" /> These bulbils are uncommon in ''[[Lilium]]'' species and they produce new plants that are [[Cloning|clones]] of the original plant.<ref name="flora-of-northamerica-online" />

The flowers are odorless.<ref name="ohwi" /> Each lasts a few days and if pollinated produces capsules with many thin seeds.<ref name="flora-of-northamerica-online" />

[[Extrafloral nectaries]] on the species were first noted by Zimmerman 1932.<ref>{{cite journal |date=2012-10-18 |first1=Marjorie G. |last1=Weber |first2=Kathleen H. |last2=Keeler |title=The phylogenetic distribution of extrafloral nectaries in plants |pages=1251–1261 |doi=10.1093/aob/mcs225 |journal=Annals of Botany |eissn=1095-8290 |volume=111 |issue=6|pmc=3662505 }}</ref>

=== Reproduction ===
These lilies are capable of both sexual and asexual reproduction, dependent on the cytotype. Some populations of the plant are diploid (have two copies of their chromosomes) and some populations are triploid (have three copies of their chromosomes). The North American population is mainly triploid, while the Asian populations may be either. The diploid populations can undergo both forms of reproduction. The triploid populations, however, are sterile and limited to asexual reproduction only. They mainly reproduce by forming bulbils in the leaf axis. <ref>{{Cite journal |last=Chung |first=Mi Yoon |last2=López-Pujol |first2=Jordi |last3=Chung |first3=Jae Min |last4=Kim |first4=Ki-Joong |last5=Park |first5=Seon Joo |last6=Chung |first6=Myong Gi |date=2015-05-01 |title=Polyploidy in Lilium lancifolium: Evidence of autotriploidy and no niche divergence between diploid and triploid cytotypes in their native ranges |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0367253015000365 |journal=Flora - Morphology, Distribution, Functional Ecology of Plants |volume=213 |pages=57–68 |doi=10.1016/j.flora.2015.04.002 |issn=0367-2530|hdl=10261/116602 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

=== Names ===

==== Scientific names ====
Botanists for many years considered ''L. tigrinum'' (after [[Ker Gawler]]<ref>[[John Bellenden Ker Gawler|Ker Gawler, J. G.]]; [[John Bellenden|Bellenden, John ]] (1809) "[https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/473123#page/2/mode/1up ''Lilium tigrinum,'' Tiger-spotted Chinese lily]". ''Botanical Magazine'' '''31''': plate 1237ff.</ref>) the correct scientific name until it was determined that older name ''L. lancifolium'' (after [[Carl Peter Thunberg|Thunberg]]<ref>Thunberg, Carl Peter (1794), [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/760193#page/369/mode/1up ''Transactions of the Linnean Society of London''] '''2''': 333 {{in lang|la}}</ref>) refers to the same species, and the latter became the accepted name.<ref name="flora-of-northamerica-online" />{{efn|Under the [[International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants|rules of international botanical nomenclature]], the older name takes precedence.}}

==== Vernacular names ====
Its common name is [[tiger lily (disambiguation)|tiger lily]]. Although this name is ambiguous across several species, it is correctly applied to this species alone.<ref name="flora-of-northamerica-online" />

== Cat toxicity ==
A case study of the successful treatment of a cat that ingested this particular species was published in 2007.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Berg |first1=Rebecca I.M. |last2=Francey |first2=Thierry |last3=Segev |first3=Gilad |title=Resolution of acute kidney injury in a cat after lily (''Lilium lancifolium'') intoxication |journal=Journal of Veterinary Internal Medicine |date=2007 |volume=21 |issue=4 |pages=857–859 |doi=10.1111/j.1939-1676.2007.tb03032.x |pmid=17708410 |url=https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1939-1676.2007.tb03032.x |doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Uses ==

It is cultivated and wild foraged in Asia for its edible [[bulb]]s.<ref name=dai-nihon-nokai/> The [[cultivar]] 'Splendens' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Lilium lancifolium'' 'Splendens'|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=3386|access-date=26 June 2013|archive-date=15 May 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130515045528/http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=3386|url-status=dead}}</ref> In Taiwan, both the flower and bulbs are used as food, as are the other related species: [[Lilium brownii var. viridulum|''L. brownii'' var. ''viridulum'']], [[Lilium pumilum|''L. pumilum'']] and ''[[Lilium candidum|L. candidum]]''.<ref>{{cite web|title=可供食品使用原料彙整一覽表|url=https://consumer.fda.gov.tw/Food/Material.aspx?nodeID=160|access-date=2014-01-25|archive-date=2014-01-26|archive-url=https://archive.today/20140126120155/https://consumer.fda.gov.tw/Food/Material.aspx?nodeID=160|url-status=dead}}</ref>
